facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant at Nicosia District Court on 10 April 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
The applicant was hit and pushed by Turkish policemen at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds.
The applicant received what she described as a 'terrible blow in the right leg beneath the tibia'.
The applicant stated that she had been hit with a sharp object, namely a bayonet wielded by a Turkish soldier.
The applicant's leg started to bleed profusely after she was struck.
The applicant felt herself drifting into unconsciousness after being struck.
The applicant shouted: 'Help, help, please, I am losing my leg'.
Some demonstrators put the applicant on a stretcher after she was struck.
The applicant was taken by ambulance to Nicosia General Hospital after being struck at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as occurring where five or more persons assemble with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conduct themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that it is immaterial that the original assembly was lawful if, being assembled, the persons conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that when an unlawful assembly has begun to execute its purpose by a breach of the peace and to the terror of the public, the assembly is called a riot and the persons assembled are said to be riotously assembled.
According to section 71 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, any person who takes part in an unlawful assembly is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment for one year.

Section 80 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that any person who carries in public without lawful occasion any offensive arm or weapon in such a manner as to cause terror to any person is guilty of a misdemeanour and is liable to imprisonment for two years, and his arms or weapons shall be forfeited.
According to section 82 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, it is an offence to carry a knife outside the home.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(b) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any police officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who commits in his presence any offence punishable with imprisonment.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(c) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any police officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who obstructs a police officer while in the execution of his duty.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration and were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.

The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' ('TRNC').
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
